questions.question: An adult meets the other prerequisites for a 2023 US BD/DNC evaluation and has no chronic CO2 retention. Which apnea-test preparation is appropriate?
options: PaCO2 35–45 mmHg, pH 7.35–7.45 and preoxygenation to PaO2 above 200 mmHg
PaCO2 25–30 mmHg, pH 7.45–7.50 and preoxygenation to PaO2 above 200 mmHg
PaCO2 35–45 mmHg, pH 7.35–7.45 and preoxygenation to PaO2 above 100 mmHg
PaCO2 45–55 mmHg, pH 7.30–7.35 and preoxygenation to PaO2 above 200 mmHg
questions.explanation:
Preparation for a Safe Apnea Test

Correct answer: PaCO2 35–45 mmHg, pH 7.35–7.45 and preoxygenation to PaO2 above 200 mmHg

Confirm Readiness Before Testing

**Without chronic CO2 retention, establish PaCO2 35–45 mmHg and pH 7.35–7.45** before the test under the 2023 US guideline.

Preoxygenate with 100% oxygen for at least ten minutes, aiming for PaO2 above 200 mmHg, and ensure the patient is not hypovolemic, hypotensive or hypoxemic.

Use an appropriate arterial sampling and monitoring plan, trained personnel and equipment to restore ventilation immediately if needed.

Maintain Oxygenation While Observing Respiratory Effort

**Use a guideline-supported oxygenation method**, selected for the patient and available expertise. Avoid unrecognized ventilator autocycling or a technique that obscures genuine respiratory effort.

Observe the chest and abdomen carefully and obtain arterial gases at appropriate times. The elapsed minutes alone do not establish a completed test.

Chronic hypercapnia, ECMO and substantial pulmonary disease require specific technical consideration rather than a generic disconnection protocol. If safe performance is not possible, follow the defined ancillary pathway. Do not start an unsafe test simply to complete a form; adequate prerequisites and a clear stopping plan are part of a valid examination.

questions.explanation:
The US Apnea Endpoint Requires Both CO2 and pH Criteria

Correct answer: PaCO2 62 mmHg with pH 7.25

Apply Every Endpoint Condition

**With no respiratory effort, the 2023 US framework requires pH below 7.30 and PaCO2 at least 60 mmHg and at least 20 mmHg above baseline.** All conditions must be satisfied.

From a baseline of 40, a final PaCO2 of 62 is a rise of 22 mmHg. Together with pH 7.25 it meets the biochemical stimulus described.

Meeting these numbers does not complete the entire death determination if other prerequisites or examination components are unmet.

**Known chronic CO2 retention requires reference to the patient’s known chronic baseline**, not an assumed normal value created by ventilator settings.

A genuine spontaneous breath prevents an apnea result consistent with BD/DNC regardless of gas values. Continue safety monitoring throughout and stop for defined instability. questions.question: During an apnea test under the 2023 US protocol, oxygen saturation progressively falls below 85% before an adequate endpoint gas is documented. Which next action is appropriate?
options: Restore ventilation and restart immediately using the same oxygenation method
Increase oxygen delivery and continue apnea until the scheduled blood gas
End testing and use the most recent gas irrespective of its CO2 and pH
Stop, restore oxygenation and reassess a safe repeat or ancillary study
questions.explanation:
Stop an Unsafe Apnea Test

Correct answer: Stop, restore oxygenation and reassess a safe repeat or ancillary study

Recognize Mandatory Safety Limits

**Progressive desaturation below 85% requires stopping under the 2023 US guideline.** Hypotension despite support or an unstable arrhythmia also requires interruption.

If feasible, obtain an arterial sample before restoring ventilation to determine whether the biochemical endpoint had already been reached, without delaying rescue.

A spontaneous breath is a different stopping reason: it demonstrates respiratory drive and is incompatible with the required apnea finding.

Do Not Convert an Incomplete Test Into a Diagnosis

**Restore stable physiology and identify why the test became unsafe.** Oxygenation technique, pulmonary disease and hemodynamics may permit a safer repeat after correction.

When testing cannot be safely completed, use the guideline’s defined ancillary approach and complete the clinical evaluation as far as possible.

Record the reason for stopping, observed respiratory activity and available gases. Do not invent endpoint values or assume that a severe initial injury makes missing data irrelevant. The safety and validity of the procedure are linked; preventing a test-related arrest is not an obstacle to correct determination but a requirement of responsible assessment.

Restore ventilation and restart immediately using the same oxygenation method: A repeat may be appropriate after stabilization, but the cause of desaturation and a safer technique must be addressed before exposing the patient to the same unresolved risk.

Increase oxygen delivery and continue apnea until the scheduled blood gas: Oxygen-delivery methods can be optimized before a safe repeat, but progressive saturation below the guideline’s stopping limit requires interruption rather than extending the current test.

End testing and use the most recent gas irrespective of its CO2 and pH: A gas obtained before rescue can be useful, but only an adequate endpoint establishes the result; the stem explicitly states that no adequate endpoint has been documented.

questions.question: A patient meets BD/DNC prerequisites, but severe facial injury prevents reliable assessment of required brainstem components. Which principle is appropriate under the 2023 US guideline?
options: Repeat the clinical examination after six hours and certify if the remaining components are unchanged
Complete safely assessable components and obtain an accepted ancillary study
Use a technically adequate EEG as confirmation of the otherwise compatible examination
Use an adequate apnea test to substitute for the inaccessible brainstem reflexes
questions.explanation:
Ancillary Testing Has Indications and Limits

Correct answer: Complete safely assessable components and obtain an accepted ancillary study

Use Ancillary Studies for a Defined Unresolved Question

**An examination or apnea test that cannot be completed or interpreted can justify ancillary testing.** Examples include relevant anatomic injury, unsafe apnea testing or uncertain movement origin.

Certain uncorrectable metabolic abnormalities have a defined role in this pathway. The specific oculocephalic exception discussed in the guideline should not be generalized to every missing component.

Perform and document the safe clinical portions first and ensure findings are otherwise consistent with the determination.

Preserve the Prerequisite Framework

**Ancillary tests do not replace establishing the catastrophic permanent mechanism or excluding hypothermia and high sedative effects.** They are not a shortcut for an inconvenient examination.

Choose a modality accepted by the stated guideline and interpreted by qualified personnel with an adequate technical study. A nondiagnostic result does not establish death.

Local law and authorized institutional protocols determine applicability. If clinical findings show consciousness, a brainstem reflex or spontaneous breathing, stop the determination rather than seeking another test to negate it. Clearly document the indication, limitations and interpretation so that the study answers the actual unresolved question.

Repeat the clinical examination after six hours and certify if the remaining components are unchanged: Repeat assessment can establish consistency, but passage of time does not resolve the required brainstem components that facial injury prevents assessing.

Use a technically adequate EEG as confirmation of the otherwise compatible examination: EEG can characterize cortical activity, but it is not accepted as an ancillary BD/DNC study under this guideline because it does not establish brainstem failure.

Use an adequate apnea test to substitute for the inaccessible brainstem reflexes: Apnea testing assesses respiratory drive, not every required cranial reflex; a completed apnea component does not eliminate the ancillary indication created by the remaining untestable components.

questions.question: An adult meets BD/DNC prerequisites, but apnea testing remains unsafe despite optimization. Under the 2023 US consensus guideline, which available investigation is accepted for this ancillary indication?
options: CT angiography using the local stroke acquisition protocol
Technically adequate transcranial Doppler ultrasonography interpreted by an experienced examiner
MR angiography with diffusion-weighted brain imaging
Continuous EEG reviewed for electrocerebral inactivity
questions.explanation:
Selecting an Accepted Adult Ancillary Perfusion Study

Correct answer: Technically adequate transcranial Doppler ultrasonography interpreted by an experienced examiner

Match the Modality to the Stated Guideline

**Accepted adult modalities include conventional four-vessel catheter angiography, radionuclide perfusion imaging and transcranial Doppler.** Availability alone does not establish diagnostic validity.

TCD requires characteristic circulatory-arrest waveforms; failure to obtain a signal through an inadequate acoustic window is not equivalent to demonstrating arrested flow.

The pediatric distinction matters: the guideline accepts TCD in adults, not children. Each modality requires appropriate acquisition and expert interpretation.

Document the Unresolved Clinical Component

**Record why ancillary testing is necessary and complete the safe examination components first.** A nondiagnostic study requires reassessment, rather than a declaration based on presumed severity.

Confirm that prerequisites remain satisfied at the time of investigation. Ancillary testing cannot override observed brain-mediated function or bypass unresolved sedative effects.

Specify jurisdiction when teaching this selection: a modality accepted elsewhere is not automatically accepted under this guideline. In clinical practice, use the legally applicable institutional pathway and retain the technical report with the determination record. The ordering clinician should communicate the precise diagnostic question to the interpreting specialist; a routine vascular study obtained for a different indication may not answer it.

Modality | 2023 US ancillary status

Conventional four-vessel catheter angiography | Accepted

Radionuclide perfusion imaging | Accepted with appropriate technique

Transcranial Doppler | Accepted in adults; not accepted in children

EEG, AEP or SEP | Not accepted

CTA; MRI/MRA | Not accepted

CT angiography using the local stroke acquisition protocol: CTA evaluates arterial anatomy and stroke occlusion, but the 2023 US guideline does not accept it as a BD/DNC ancillary test because validation is insufficient.

MR angiography with diffusion-weighted brain imaging: MRI and MRA can characterize injury and vessels, but are not accepted ancillary modalities in this guideline because adequate validation is lacking.

Continuous EEG reviewed for electrocerebral inactivity: EEG is valuable for seizures and cortical activity, but does not establish loss of brainstem function and is not accepted for this ancillary indication.

questions.question: An ICU patient has electrocerebral inactivity on a technically adequate EEG. Under the 2023 US BD/DNC guideline, which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: It does not establish brainstem failure or replace the required assessment
It can serve as the ancillary study when the apnea test is unsafe
It becomes an accepted ancillary study if auditory evoked potentials are also absent
It can substitute for serial clinical assessment once hypothermia is excluded
questions.explanation:
Electrical Silence Does Not Establish Brainstem Failure

Correct answer: It does not establish brainstem failure or replace the required assessment

Understand What the Recording Samples

**Scalp EEG primarily evaluates cerebral cortical electrical activity.** Electrical silence does not establish absence of every brainstem function.

The 2023 US guideline therefore does not accept EEG, auditory evoked potentials or somatosensory evoked potentials as ancillary tests for this purpose.

This restriction concerns death determination, not the usefulness of EEG for seizures, encephalopathy or selected prognostic questions.

Keep Diagnostic Questions Separate

**An investigation must answer the clinical question being asked.** A technically excellent recording can still be unsuitable for a different diagnostic purpose.

Record the indication, relevant medicines, temperature and physiologic conditions when interpreting electrophysiology. Describe the observed finding without extending it beyond the test’s domain.

If a required clinical component cannot be assessed safely, establish the indication for an accepted ancillary modality rather than relabeling a previously obtained EEG. Communicate clearly with families: lack of detectable cortical activity on one recording is not, by itself, a complete declaration of death. Conversely, a test obtained for seizure monitoring should be interpreted according to its own clinical purpose, with appropriate attention to artifact and technical adequacy.

It can serve as the ancillary study when the apnea test is unsafe: This was accepted in some older frameworks, but the 2023 US guideline does not accept EEG for this purpose because it does not assess brainstem function.

It becomes an accepted ancillary study if auditory evoked potentials are also absent: Adding tests of restricted pathways does not overcome the incomplete assessment of the entire brainstem; this combination is not accepted by the stated guideline.

It can substitute for serial clinical assessment once hypothermia is excluded: Excluding hypothermia addresses one prerequisite, but does not convert a cortical electrical recording into the required comprehensive clinical or accepted ancillary determination.

questions.question: Under the adult minimum interval explicitly specified in Indian Form 10, when may the second brain-stem death examination follow the first?

At least six hours later
At least twelve hours later
At least twenty-four hours later
questions.explanation:

Correct answer: At least six hours later

Identify the Jurisdiction Before Applying an Interval

Document the actual dates and times, examination findings, applicable prerequisites and the identity of the examining board.

Do not import a different country’s adult examination rule simply because its clinical guideline is more familiar.

Use the Interval as One Part of Certification

**An observation interval is not an independent diagnostic test.** The underlying cause, exclusion of reversible confounders and required clinical assessment remain essential.

If sedation, hypothermia, hemodynamic instability or another unresolved factor prevents valid testing, address that factor rather than scheduling a second invalid examination.

Separate the timing of the examinations from subsequent administrative tasks and any discussion of donation. A family’s decision about donation cannot shorten the required assessment. Similarly, a transfer between hospitals does not justify reconstructing undocumented findings from memory: obtain the original records and follow the authorized local process. Numerical examination questions should name the governing form or guideline because superficially similar questions may have different answers across jurisdictions.

questions.question: Which group corresponds to the four positions listed for signatures on Indian Form 10, before considering its authorized substitution provision?
options: Hospital medical administrator, authorized specialist, anesthetist and treating medical officer
Hospital medical administrator, transplant coordinator, neurologist/neurosurgeon and treating medical officer
Hospital medical administrator, authorized specialist, neurologist/neurosurgeon and recipient surgeon
Hospital medical administrator, authorized specialist, neurologist/neurosurgeon and treating medical officer
questions.explanation:

Correct answer: Hospital medical administrator, authorized specialist, neurologist/neurosurgeon and treating medical officer

Recognize the Listed Positions

**Form 10 lists the administrator, authorized specialist, neurologist/neurosurgeon and treating medical officer.** Its panel and substitution notes must also be followed.

The authorized specialist and neurologist/neurosurgeon positions are co-opted from a hospital-nominated panel approved by the Appropriate Authority.

When neurologic specialists are unavailable, the form provides a nomination pathway involving a surgeon or physician and an anesthetist or intensivist; it is not unrestricted replacement by any available doctor.

**Check the current approved panel and applicable institutional implementation.** Clinical expertise and legal authorization are related requirements but are not interchangeable.

A coordinator may help assemble documentation and support the family, but administrative assistance does not transfer medical certification responsibility. questions.question: A team proposes automatically using the adult six-hour minimum for every child because it appears on Indian Form 10. Which response best reflects the form’s pediatric qualification?
options: Use twenty-four hours for every infant because Form 10 specifies that fixed infant interval
Use the adult six-hour minimum for children older than one year
Use twelve hours for every child because Form 10 specifies that fixed pediatric interval
Increase the interval according to the BSD experts and applicable pediatric protocol
questions.explanation:
Pediatric Intervals Require an Age-Specific Protocol

Correct answer: Increase the interval according to the BSD experts and applicable pediatric protocol

Read the Pediatric Qualification Explicitly

**Form 10 calls for increased intervals in children and infants according to the BSD experts’ opinion.** It does not provide one universal pediatric numeric interval.

Its age categories include children aged 6–12 years, those aged 1–5 years and infants. Apply the current authorized pediatric pathway to the actual age and circumstances.

Do not silently replace this wording with a foreign society guideline and describe the imported numbers as the text of Indian law.

Distinguish a Legal Form From a Clinical Recommendation

**Document which recommendation and institutional protocol support the chosen interval.** When requirements differ, resolve the applicable process before certification.

Prematurity, very young age, injury mechanism and unresolved confounders require particular attention from experienced pediatric clinicians.

A longer observation period cannot compensate for an uncertain diagnosis or an uninterpretable examination. Explain to the family why repeated assessment is necessary and what remains to be established. Avoid giving a promised declaration time before prerequisites are met. For examination preparation, retain both the adult minimum and the explicit pediatric qualification; memorizing one number for every age creates a clinically important error even when the adult answer itself is correct.

Use twenty-four hours for every infant because Form 10 specifies that fixed infant interval: Longer age-specific observation may be recommended in a pediatric protocol, but the form’s own wording leaves increased intervals to the experts rather than stating this universal infant number.

Use the adult six-hour minimum for children older than one year: The form explicitly includes pediatric age categories in its increased-interval qualification; the adult minimum cannot simply be extended to every child above one year.

Use twelve hours for every child because Form 10 specifies that fixed pediatric interval: A twelve-hour interval appears in some clinical recommendations, but Form 10 itself does not specify one fixed numeric interval for all pediatric ages.

questions.question: The family of an Indian ICU patient undergoing brain-stem death assessment declines organ donation. Which approach to the medical assessment is appropriate?
options: Transfer responsibility for final certification to the donation coordinator
Defer certification while arranging another donation-counseling discussion
Use a non-donor certification pathway that omits repeat brainstem testing
Continue the valid medical assessment and provide family support independently of donation authorization
questions.explanation:
Certification and Donation Are Separate Decisions

Correct answer: Continue the valid medical assessment and provide family support independently of donation authorization

Maintain Independent Medical Determination

**Certification depends on the prescribed clinical findings and authorized process.** A donation preference cannot supply missing examination findings or negate valid ones.

Record the cause, exclusion of confounders, prerequisites, examination and apnea-test findings, dates, times and required signatures accurately.

Use the applicable Indian form and institutional pathway. Unresolved components must be addressed through an authorized process rather than hidden in a completed checklist.

Explain the Findings With Care

**Families need a clear account of what has been assessed and what it means.** Avoid using donation language as the explanation for the medical diagnosis.

Allow questions, check understanding and distinguish ongoing ventilator-supported circulation from recovery of brain function. Describe uncertainty honestly if the determination is incomplete.

Donation requires its own appropriate authorization and coordination. Family support remains necessary regardless of the decision. A coordinator can assist with logistics and communication while the certifying team retains responsibility for findings and records. Do not promise recipients or organ availability before the relevant processes are complete. Accurate documentation should allow another authorized clinician to reconstruct the sequence from contemporaneous evidence, without relying on informal recollection or assumptions about why assessment was initiated.

Transfer responsibility for final certification to the donation coordinator: Coordinators may assist with logistics and communication, but the authorized medical board retains responsibility for the determination and its findings.

Defer certification while arranging another donation-counseling discussion: Further counseling may support an informed decision, but donation authorization does not determine whether clinically indicated death assessment should proceed.

Use a non-donor certification pathway that omits repeat brainstem testing: The family’s retrieval preference does not create permission to omit the required examination or documentation in the stated certification process.

questions.question: A malnourished adult with prolonged heavy alcohol use develops confusion and a broad-based gait. Eye movements are normal. Glucose has been corrected, but symptoms persist. Which next approach is most appropriate?
options: Begin oral thiamine replacement with nutritional rehabilitation
Begin treatment-dose IV thiamine while investigating other causes
Begin prevention-dose parenteral thiamine during alcohol-withdrawal treatment
Obtain brain MRI and then select parenteral treatment according to the result
questions.explanation:
Wernicke Encephalopathy Without the Complete Triad

Correct answer: Begin treatment-dose IV thiamine while investigating other causes

Recognize an Incomplete Clinical Presentation

**Confusion, gait ataxia and ocular abnormalities need not all be present.** Malnutrition and compatible neurologic findings warrant a low threshold for treatment.

Consider dietary deficiency, eye signs, cerebellar dysfunction and altered mental state or memory impairment together; the complete classic triad is an insensitive requirement.

MRI can support the diagnosis but does not replace clinical judgment. Check for infection, withdrawal, intoxication, structural disease and metabolic contributors in parallel.

Separate Treatment From Prophylaxis

**Suspected symptomatic Wernicke encephalopathy requires parenteral therapy.** UK guidance recommends ==thiamine 300–500 mg IV three times daily for 3–5 days==, with daily review.

If still symptomatic after five days, that guidance uses 300–500 mg IV once daily for a further 3–5 days and while improvement continues. Regimens differ between authorities; state the regimen being used.

Correct magnesium deficiency and nutritional deficits, monitor the response and follow parenteral-administration precautions. Do not delay emergency glucose for hypoglycemia while arranging thiamine. Prevention doses are not interchangeable with treatment of established neurologic disease. After the acute course, provide ongoing supplementation and nutritional and alcohol-use care; residual memory impairment may persist despite improvement in eye signs or gait.

Begin oral thiamine replacement with nutritional rehabilitation: Oral replacement is useful after acute therapy or in selected prevention settings, but suspected symptomatic Wernicke encephalopathy requires prompt parenteral treatment.

Begin prevention-dose parenteral thiamine during alcohol-withdrawal treatment: Prevention is appropriate in at-risk patients without compatible neurologic disease, but this patient’s persistent confusion and ataxia warrant a treatment regimen.

Obtain brain MRI and then select parenteral treatment according to the result: MRI can support diagnosis and identify alternatives, but sensitivity is insufficient to exclude Wernicke encephalopathy and imaging should not delay empirical treatment.

questions.explanation:
Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome

Correct answer: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome

Interpret the Clinicoradiographic Pattern

**PRES combines acute neurologic symptoms with predominantly vasogenic edema.** Increased ADC supports extracellular edema; restricted diffusion can indicate superimposed injury.

Hypertension, renal dysfunction, eclampsia and endothelial-toxic medicines are important settings. Posterior predominance is characteristic but neither exclusive nor mandatory.

Hemorrhage, infarction and persistent deficits can occur; the word reversible does not guarantee a benign outcome.

Treat the Precipitant and Immediate Complications

**Control seizures and reduce severe blood pressure with monitored, titratable treatment.** Avoid abrupt excessive lowering that compromises cerebral perfusion.

Review tacrolimus exposure, drug interactions, renal function and the immunosuppression plan with the transplant team rather than stopping essential therapy without a replacement strategy.

Evaluate atypical findings for arterial or venous ischemia, infection and other competing diagnoses. Repeat clinical assessment and follow-up imaging can document the evolution. A normal early CT does not exclude the MRI-defined syndrome. In a patient with persistent impaired awareness after convulsions, obtain EEG to assess ongoing seizures. Recovery and the duration of antiseizure treatment depend on the injury and clinical course, rather than an assumption that every patient needs indefinite therapy.

Bilateral posterior cerebral artery infarction: PCA infarction can cause visual loss, but acute cytotoxic ischemia typically restricts diffusion and follows an arterial distribution rather than the stated vasogenic edema pattern.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: Immunosuppression raises this possibility, but its usually progressive focal course and asymmetric white-matter injury fit less well than an acute hypertensive seizure syndrome.

questions.explanation:
Serotonin Toxicity and Neuromuscular Excitation

Correct answer: Serotonin toxicity

Integrate Exposure With the Examination

**Clonus and hyperreflexia are major discriminators in a compatible serotonergic exposure.** Review recent starts, dose escalation, interactions and overdose rather than considering each prescription separately.

With serotonergic exposure, Hunter patterns include spontaneous clonus; inducible or ocular clonus with agitation or diaphoresis; tremor with hyperreflexia; or hypertonia with temperature above 38°C and ocular or inducible clonus.

Severe rigidity can mask clonus. Do not dismiss a critically ill patient because a complete textbook pattern is difficult to elicit.

Reduce Muscle Activity and Prevent Organ Injury

**Stop serotonergic contributors and provide monitored supportive care.** Benzodiazepines, active cooling, fluids and management of complications are central.

Severe hyperthermia with rigidity may require airway control, ventilation and nondepolarizing paralysis. Antipyretics do not address heat generated by excessive muscular activity.

Cyproheptadine is an enteral adjunct, not a substitute for resuscitation; Austin guidance uses 12 mg initially then 2 mg every two hours until response. Evidence for outcome benefit is limited. Discuss severe cases with toxicology, monitor CK, renal function and electrolytes, and assess coingestants. Reintroduction of psychiatric therapy requires review of the interaction, washout and clinical recovery rather than immediate resumption of the previous combination.

Antimuscarinic toxicity: Antimuscarinic poisoning can cause agitation, hyperthermia and mydriasis, but typically produces dry skin and reduced bowel activity rather than diaphoresis, diarrhea and clonus.

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: NMS usually follows dopamine blockade or withdrawal of dopaminergic therapy and favors generalized rigidity; the rapid serotonergic interaction with clonus and hyperreflexia is more characteristic of serotonin toxicity.

Malignant catatonia: Malignant catatonia combines catatonic signs with systemic instability and may precede drug exposure; this abrupt interaction-related neuromuscular excitation is more consistent with serotonin toxicity.

questions.explanation:
Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome Requires Withdrawal and Support

Correct answer: Withdraw dopamine blockers and provide intensive cooling, fluids and organ monitoring

Recognize a Drug-Associated Systemic Emergency

**NMS is associated with dopamine antagonism and can also follow abrupt withdrawal of dopaminergic treatment.** Medication chronology and examination help distinguish it from other hyperthermic syndromes.

Raised CK supports muscle injury but is neither specific nor mandatory. Check electrolytes, renal function, urine output and complications of rhabdomyolysis.

Investigate infection, seizures, heat illness and other mimics when indicated; a suspected medicine reaction does not exclude a concurrent illness.

Escalate According to Severity

**Withdrawal of the trigger and intensive supportive treatment are foundational.** Address airway safety, temperature, circulating volume and organ dysfunction promptly.

BAP guidance supports specialist consideration of lorazepam, dopamine agonists or dantrolene according to severity; ECT can be relevant for persistent severe disease or catatonic features. These are not interchangeable mandatory antidotes.

Evidence is largely observational. Drug choice must consider contraindications and organ function, with close clinical monitoring. Prevent aspiration, thrombosis and pressure injury while immobility persists. After recovery, reassess whether an antipsychotic remains necessary, allow an appropriate recovery interval and use a cautious specialist-supervised strategy if restarting. Record the reaction and avoid recreating the same rapid escalation and dehydration risks.

Withdraw dopamine blockers and prioritize enteral cyproheptadine treatment: Trigger withdrawal is appropriate, but cyproheptadine targets serotonin toxicity and is not the principal treatment for this dopamine-blockade-associated syndrome.

Withdraw dopamine blockers and use bromocriptine before arranging intensive support: Bromocriptine may be considered as a specialist adjunct, but the severe hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis require immediate systemic support rather than waiting for a drug response.

Withdraw dopamine blockers and use antipyretics before deciding on active cooling: Withdrawal is necessary, but antipyretics do not adequately address muscle-related heat production; severe hyperthermia requires prompt active cooling and organ support.

BAP evidence-based consensus guideline on catatonia, 2023 — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10101189/

questions.explanation:
Malignant Catatonia and Early ECT Planning

Correct answer: Monitored lorazepam and urgent ECT assessment with systemic support

Recognize Malignant Physiology in Catatonia

**Fever and autonomic instability accompanying catatonic motor and behavioral signs indicate a medical emergency.** Catatonia may occur with psychiatric, neurologic or systemic disease.

Assess for encephalitis, seizures, medication effects or withdrawal and metabolic illness. The chronology before dopamine blockade helps distinguish the presentation from typical drug-triggered NMS, although overlap exists.

Support hydration, nutrition, airway safety and renal function; immobility also requires thrombosis and pressure-injury prevention.

Treat While Investigating the Cause

**Lorazepam and ECT are key treatments, with urgent ECT planning in malignant disease.** A monitored 1–2 mg IV lorazepam challenge can support assessment, but a negative response does not exclude catatonia.

BAP guidance recommends ECT if response to lorazepam is partial or absent within 48–72 hours; rapid deterioration warrants urgent escalation rather than waiting for the full interval.

Further benzodiazepine dosing requires individualized titration and respiratory monitoring. Coordinate psychiatry, neurology, anesthesia and critical care early, including capacity and consent processes under applicable law. Treat an identified underlying cause in parallel. The evidence base includes substantial observational experience rather than large definitive trials, so communicate anticipated benefit and risks honestly while avoiding delay in a potentially fatal syndrome.

High-dose antipsychotic treatment with intensive temperature control: Antipsychotics may be used for selected psychiatric syndromes, but can worsen catatonia and precipitate NMS; systemic cooling does not remove that risk.

Monitored lorazepam with ECT assessment deferred until a week-long trial is complete: Lorazepam is appropriate, but malignant physiology requires early ECT planning and escalation within 48–72 hours for inadequate response, or sooner with deterioration.

Immunotherapy first, with catatonia-specific treatment after antibody confirmation: Autoimmune encephalitis must be considered and may need parallel treatment, but antibody testing should not delay treatment of the immediately dangerous catatonic syndrome.

questions.question: After two weeks of sepsis and ventilation, a patient is awake, follows commands and has symmetric flaccid limb weakness with difficulty weaning. Sensory nerve action potentials and motor response amplitudes are reduced without a demyelinating pattern. Which mechanism best fits?
options: Critical illness myopathy
Critical illness polyneuropathy
Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy
Myasthenic crisis
questions.explanation:
ICU-Acquired Weakness After Critical Illness

Correct answer: Critical illness polyneuropathy

Localize Weakness Separately From Consciousness

**ICU-acquired weakness may reflect polyneuropathy, myopathy or both.** A patient can understand commands yet lack the motor strength to demonstrate a normal examination.

Assess strength when cooperation is adequate. The MRC sum evaluates six bilateral muscle groups, each scored 0–5, for a total of 60; a score below 48 commonly defines significant ICU-acquired weakness.

Sedation, delirium, pain and poor cooperation limit manual testing. Review electrolytes, medication effects and other neurologic causes before attributing weakness to critical illness.

Use Electrophysiology for the Relevant Distinction

**Reduced sensory and motor amplitudes support axonal polyneuropathy.** Preserved sensory responses with myopathic findings support myopathy, although overlap is common.

Nerve conduction studies, needle EMG and sometimes direct muscle stimulation help clarify the mechanism when the result will inform care.

Treat the underlying critical illness, optimize nutrition and mobilization as tolerated, and plan respiratory and functional rehabilitation. A label of ICU-acquired weakness does not eliminate the need to investigate atypical asymmetry, cranial findings, a sensory level or evolving weakness. Prognosis depends on the injury, comorbidity and rehabilitation trajectory. Avoid interpreting an inability to lift the limbs as evidence of absent awareness, particularly during discussions of recovery and goals of care.

Critical illness myopathy: Myopathy can produce symmetric weakness and weaning failure, but sensory responses are generally preserved; reduced sensory amplitudes favor an axonal neuropathic component here.

Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy: AIDP can cause flaccid weakness and respiratory failure, but typically shows demyelinating electrophysiologic features; the stated axonal pattern after prolonged sepsis favors critical illness polyneuropathy.

Myasthenic crisis: Myasthenia can impair ventilation and limb strength, but sensory nerve responses remain normal and neuromuscular transmission studies, rather than an axonal sensory pattern, support that diagnosis.

questions.explanation:
Minimally Conscious State Requires Reproducible Evidence

Correct answer: Minimally conscious state

Separate Arousal From Awareness

**Minimally conscious state includes definite but limited evidence of awareness.** Responses may fluctuate, so repeat standardized assessment rather than relying on one brief encounter.

Unresponsive wakefulness syndrome has eye opening and sleep–wake cycles without demonstrated awareness. Coma lacks wakefulness; neither term is synonymous with death by neurologic criteria.

Functional communication or appropriate functional object use supports emergence from minimally conscious state, which is a separate threshold from occasional command following.

Optimize the Opportunity to Demonstrate Awareness

**Use a validated instrument such as the Coma Recovery Scale–Revised and address confounders.** Sedatives, sleep disruption, seizures and systemic illness can lower performance.

Motor, visual, auditory and language limitations can hide awareness. Adapt the examination, assess serially and involve clinicians experienced in disorders of consciousness.

Explain the distinction between current diagnostic category and individual prognosis to the family. Continue pain assessment, rehabilitation and prevention of immobility complications. Specialist testing may be considered when behavior and other evidence are discordant, but an isolated test should not be stretched beyond its validated interpretation. Document which response was observed, its reproducibility and the conditions of testing so that apparent changes can be evaluated rather than inferred from inconsistent labels.

Coma | Absent | Absent

Unresponsive wakefulness syndrome | Present | Not demonstrated

Minimally conscious state | Present | Definite but limited; may fluctuate

Emergence from minimally conscious state | Present | Functional communication or functional object use

Classic locked-in syndrome | Present | Preserved; demonstrated through suitable communication

Unresponsive wakefulness syndrome: This syndrome includes wakefulness without behavioral evidence of awareness; reproducible command following provides evidence beyond reflexive wakefulness.

Coma: Coma lacks wakefulness as well as awareness; established sleep–wake cycles and intermittent command following are inconsistent with ongoing coma.

Emergence from minimally conscious state: Emergence requires reliable functional communication or functional object use; intermittent simple command following establishes awareness but not that higher threshold.

questions.question: A patient has recurrent leg weakness and an appropriate structural evaluation. Repeated examination shows a convincing Hoover sign without new acute red flags. Which next management approach is most appropriate?
options: Refer for psychological treatment without explaining the examination findings
Repeat brain and spinal MRI before discussing the diagnosis
Explain the positive clinical diagnosis and arrange functional motor rehabilitation
Offer reassurance and discharge without a rehabilitation or follow-up plan
questions.explanation:
Functional Weakness Requires Positive Clinical Evidence

Correct answer: Explain the positive clinical diagnosis and arrange functional motor rehabilitation

Make a Positive Clinical Diagnosis

**Hoover sign demonstrates a discrepancy between voluntary and automatic hip extension.** Interpret it in the context of pain, comprehension and the rest of the examination.

Other presentations require their own appropriate positive signs; one motor sign is not a universal test for every functional symptom.

A psychiatric history, stressor or normal scan is insufficient by itself. Symptoms can be disabling and involuntary even when their mechanism differs from a structural lesion.

Explain the Finding and Address the Actual Disability

**Show how the examination supports the diagnosis and offer a treatment plan.** Use clear, respectful language that validates symptoms and describes potential for improvement.

Specialist physiotherapy can retrain movement; psychological treatment and management of pain, fatigue or psychiatric comorbidity may be useful according to the individual presentation.

Keep acute red flags in view: a new focal syndrome, altered consciousness, sphincter dysfunction or a changed examination may warrant renewed investigation. A previous functional diagnosis must not become a reason to dismiss a later illness. Avoid repeated nondirected testing once the diagnosis is well supported, while providing follow-up and an explanation of when reassessment is appropriate. Rehabilitation goals should focus on restoring function and confidence rather than requiring the patient to accept a psychological cause as a prerequisite for care.

Refer for psychological treatment without explaining the examination findings: Psychological care can help selected patients, but omitting the positive neurologic explanation leaves the diagnosis unsupported to the patient and neglects motor rehabilitation.

Repeat brain and spinal MRI before discussing the diagnosis: Repeat imaging is warranted for new red flags or an inadequately evaluated localization, but indiscriminate repetition after an appropriate assessment delays a positive diagnosis and rehabilitation.

Offer reassurance and discharge without a rehabilitation or follow-up plan: Reassurance is valuable, but functional weakness can cause substantial disability; a supported diagnosis, treatment pathway and appropriate follow-up are needed.

Australian health-professional recommendations for functional neurological disorder, 2025 — https://neurologyopen.bmj.com/content/7/1/e000970
